pos: n. (a Benjamite who settled in Jerusalem after the return; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Gabbai, of uncertain sense, perhaps a tax-gatherer or a collector; named once, Nehemiah 11:8.
biblical_def: Gabbai is named once, in the roll of those who took up residence in the rebuilt city: “And after him Gabbai, Sallai, nine hundred twenty and eight” (Nehemiah 11:8). The chapter records a difficulty that few readers expect. The wall was finished and the city was empty: “Now the city was large and great: but the people were few therein, and the houses were not builded” (Nehemiah 7:4). Living in Jerusalem meant leaving a farm for a ruin, and so the matter was settled by lot: “And the rulers of the people dwelt at Jerusalem: the rest of the people also cast lots, to bring one of ten to dwell in Jerusalem the holy city, and nine parts to dwell in other cities” (Nehemiah 11:1). And the verse that follows is the heart of the chapter: “And the people blessed all the men, that willingly offered themselves to dwell at Jerusalem” (Nehemiah 11:2). Some drew the lot and some volunteered, and the congregation blessed the volunteers. Gabbai stands in that company, one of nine hundred twenty-eight Benjamites who made the holy city their home when it was a hard place to live.

corruption_summary: Nehemiah is read as a manual of leadership technique, where the book's own account turns on prayer, obedience and willing sacrifice.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah has been mined for decades as a leadership handbook: vision-casting, stakeholder management, project phases, opposition handling. The book does contain wise administration, and a reader who takes only that has taken the husk. Nehemiah's first act is a month of fasting and confession; his method at every crisis is to pray a sentence and act; and the repopulation of Jerusalem is accomplished not by incentive but by lot and by men offering themselves, with the congregation pronouncing a blessing on them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's work is usually costly to somebody in particular. The walls were up and the city was still empty, because a rebuilt wall does not feed a family. Gabbai's name is in Scripture because he moved into a city that needed inhabitants, and the people blessed the men who did it.

pos: n. (a son of Jahdai in the house of Caleb; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Geshan, of uncertain sense, perhaps lumpy or a clod; named once, 1 Chronicles 2:47.
biblical_def: Geshan occurs once: “And the sons of Jahdai; Regem, and Jotham, and Geshan, and Pelet, and Ephah, and Shaaph” (1 Chronicles 2:47). The register is Caleb's, and the surrounding verses are an unusually frank family record: “And Ephah, Caleb's concubine, bare Haran, and Moza, and Gazez: and Haran begat Gazez” (1 Chronicles 2:46), and then, “She bare also Shaaph the father of Madmannah, Sheva the father of Machbenah, and the father of Gibea: and the daughter of Caleb was Achsah” (1 Chronicles 2:49). The Chronicler writes down the concubines and their children as plainly as the wives and theirs. The chapter had opened with the same unsparing honesty about the head of the tribe: “The sons of Judah; Er, and Onan, and Shelah: which three were born unto him of the daughter of Shua the Canaanitess. And Er, the firstborn of Judah, was evil in the sight of the LORD; and he slew him” (1 Chronicles 2:3). Geshan is a name in a register that tells the truth about the family it records, which is the mark of Scripture everywhere.

corruption_summary: Scripture's plain record of concubinage is read as approval of it, where the Bible reports the practice, never commands it, and shows its fruit.
corruption_paragraphs: That the Old Testament records concubines and polygamy without a running commentary is regularly taken to mean that it endorses them, and sometimes that biblical marriage is therefore negotiable. The books themselves answer. The pattern given at creation and reaffirmed by the Lord Jesus is one man and one woman joined for life; every polygamous household in Scripture is shown breeding rivalry, favouritism and grief — Abraham's, Jacob's, Gideon's, David's, Solomon's; and the law restrained what the hardness of men's hearts had introduced rather than instituting it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honesty of the register. The Chronicler names the concubine, names her sons, and three verses earlier notes that Judah's firstborn was evil in the sight of the LORD and was slain. A book that reports its heroes' households this way is not flattering anyone.

pos: n. (head of a family of the Nethinims who returned from Babylon; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Chagab, a locust or grasshopper; named once, Ezra 2:46, and distinct from Hagabah of the preceding verse.
biblical_def: Hagab occurs once: “The children of Hagab, the children of Shalmai, the children of Hanan” (Ezra 2:46). He is distinct from Hagabah, whose family stands in the verse before his in the same list; two similar names, two households, and the Authorized Version keeps them apart. The company he belongs to is named at the head of that section: “The Nethinims: the children of Ziha, the children of Hasupha, the children of Tabbaoth” (Ezra 2:43). The Nethinims — the word means the given ones — were the servants of the Levites in the sanctuary, and their origin is given plainly: “Also of the Nethinims, whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites, two hundred and twenty Nethinims: all of them were expressed by name” (Ezra 8:20). That last clause is worth weighing: the lowest order of temple servants was registered man by man. And they came home with everyone else: “So the priests, and the Levites, and some of the people, and the singers, and the porters, and the Nethinims, dwelt in their cities, and all Israel in their cities” (Ezra 2:70).

corruption_summary: Menial service in God's house is treated as a lesser calling, where Scripture registers the servants by name and David himself appointed them.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture that ranks work by visibility finds the Nethinims hard to place: temple servants, probably of foreign descent, doing the carrying and the drawing for the Levites. Scripture does not treat them as an underclass. Their families are listed by name in the register of the return, exactly as the priests and the singers are; Ezra notes that the two hundred and twenty with him “were expressed by name”; and the appointment is traced to David and the princes, which is to say the office was ordered and not improvised.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps the names of those who serve where nobody looks. A man called Locust headed a household of temple servants and came back from Babylon with the rest, and the Holy Ghost wrote him into the book between Shalmai and Hanan.

pos: n. (head of a family of the Nethinims who returned from Babylon; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Asnah, of uncertain sense, perhaps thornbush; named once, Ezra 2:50.
biblical_def: Asnah occurs once: “The children of Asnah, the children of Mehunim, the children of Nephusim” (Ezra 2:50). Like Hagab, he heads one household among the Nethinims, whose section of the register opens a few verses earlier: “The Nethinims: the children of Ziha, the children of Hasupha, the children of Tabbaoth” (Ezra 2:43). The office is traced to the days of the monarchy: “Also of the Nethinims, whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites, two hundred and twenty Nethinims: all of them were expressed by name” (Ezra 8:20). The whole of Ezra 2 is a list — priests by house, Levites, singers, porters, Nethinims, the children of Solomon's servants, and the men who could not prove their pedigree — and its last verse records that every order went home: “So the priests, and the Levites, and some of the people, and the singers, and the porters, and the Nethinims, dwelt in their cities, and all Israel in their cities” (Ezra 2:70). Asnah's name has survived two and a half millennia because his household came back to serve in the house of God.

corruption_summary: The lists in Ezra are skipped as archival clutter, where they were the legal proof of pedigree on which priesthood and inheritance depended.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 2 is the kind of chapter readers turn past and critics file under temple bookkeeping. Its function was weightier than that. A returning priest who could not produce his line was put from the priesthood until a decision could be made by Urim and Thummim; families who could not shew their father's house are noted as such in the same chapter. The register was not nostalgia; it decided who could serve at the altar and who held which portion of the land.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the worth God sets on the names of His servants. Asnah is a thornbush of a name in a list of temple porters' and servants' households, and it is in the word of God, which is more than can be said for the kings of Babylon who carried them away.

pos: n. (the last name in the royal genealogy of the Old Testament; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Anani, commonly explained as my cloud, or protected by the LORD, from 'anan, a cloud; named once, 1 Chronicles 3:24.
biblical_def: Anani has a distinction that no other obscure name in Scripture shares: he is the last man named in the royal line of David in the Old Testament. “And the sons of Elioenai were, Hodaiah, and Eliashib, and Pelaiah, and Akkub, and Johanan, and Dalaiah, and Anani, seven” (1 Chronicles 3:24). The chapter has come down from David through the kings, through the captivity, and on past the governor of the return: “And the sons of Pedaiah were, Zerubbabel, and Shimei: and the sons of Zerubbabel; Meshullam, and Hananiah, and Shelomith their sister” (1 Chronicles 3:19), having first noted the disaster at the centre of it: “And the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son” (1 Chronicles 3:17). Of Jeconiah the LORD had said through Jeremiah: “Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah” (Jeremiah 22:30). The line ran on and never sat on the throne again — seven brothers in a Persian province, and then silence. Matthew picks it up where the Chronicler left it: “And after they were brought to Babylon, Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel” (Matthew 1:12).

corruption_summary: The curse on Jeconiah is set against the promise to David as a contradiction, where Scripture fulfils both by the virgin birth.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a difficulty with real teeth, and it is worth stating plainly rather than evading. God swore to David that his son would sit on his throne for ever; God said of Jeconiah that no man of his seed should prosper on that throne. Both stand, and the Gospels answer them together: Christ receives the legal right to the throne through Joseph, Jeconiah's heir, and takes His flesh not from Joseph's seed but from the virgin, whose line Luke traces through Nathan and not through Jeconiah. The curse falls on the seed; the promise rests on the Son.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a genealogy can end in apparent failure and not be finished. Seven brothers in a province of Persia, the last of them called my cloud, and no throne in sight for five hundred years — and the Chronicler wrote them down because the word of God had not failed.

pos: n. (a son of Shimon in the genealogies of Judah; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Ben-chanan, son of grace, from ben, a son, and chanan, to be gracious; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:20.
biblical_def: Ben-hanan occurs once: “And the sons of Shimon were, Amnon, and Rinnah, Benhanan, and Tilon. And the sons of Ishi were, Zoheth, and Benzoheth” (1 Chronicles 4:20). His name means son of grace, and it belongs to the long Judahite register of 1 Chronicles 4, which opens with the tribe's head: “The sons of Judah; Pharez, Hezron, and Carmi, and Hur, and Shobal” (1 Chronicles 4:1). The chapter is a list with one famous interruption in it, where a man's prayer and God's answer are recorded between two columns of names: “And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested” (1 Chronicles 4:10). The verse after Ben-hanan's names the trade of a whole household: “The sons of Shelah the son of Judah were, Er the father of Lecah, and Laadah the father of Mareshah, and the families of the house of them that wrought fine linen, of the house of Ashbea” (1 Chronicles 4:21). A son of grace, named once, among weavers and pray-ers and men whose names are all we have.

corruption_summary: Grace is redefined as unconditional acceptance of a man as he is, where Scripture makes it God's unmerited favour that both forgives and changes.
corruption_paragraphs: The word grace has been emptied and refilled in our time. In common use it now means acceptance without condition or correction — a disposition to approve. Scripture means something far better and far more costly: the free favour of God toward those who deserve wrath, purchased at the cross, given without respect to merit, and never given alone. The same grace that justifies teaches men to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts. A grace that leaves a man unchanged is not the grace of the New Testament.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the name. Some father in Judah called his son son of grace, and the Chronicler wrote it down. Whatever the man was, his name confessed that what a household has it has received, and that is the doctrine the Reformation recovered out of the same word.

pos: n. (a son of Ishi in the genealogies of Judah; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Ben-zocheth, son of Zoheth, from ben, a son; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:20, beside Zoheth his father or brother.
biblical_def: Ben-zoheth occurs once, at the end of the same verse that gives Ben-hanan: “And the sons of Shimon were, Amnon, and Rinnah, Benhanan, and Tilon. And the sons of Ishi were, Zoheth, and Benzoheth” (1 Chronicles 4:20). The construction is unusual: Zoheth and Ben-zoheth, that is Zoheth and the son of Zoheth, are named together as sons of Ishi, and the Authorized Version renders what the Hebrew has without smoothing the oddity away. The register belongs to Judah: “The sons of Judah; Pharez, Hezron, and Carmi, and Hur, and Shobal” (1 Chronicles 4:1), and the chapter's one narrative moment stands a few verses above: “And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested” (1 Chronicles 4:10). Immediately after comes a household known by its craft: “the families of the house of them that wrought fine linen, of the house of Ashbea” (1 Chronicles 4:21). These are the fathers and trades of the tribe from which Christ came.

corruption_summary: An awkward construction is smoothed away by emendation, where a faithful version renders the Hebrew and lets the reader see the difficulty.
corruption_paragraphs: Zoheth and Ben-zoheth named as two sons of one father is grammatically odd, and modern treatments commonly emend it, supplying a name or reading the second as a scribal repetition. That may be discussed; it is not translation. The Authorized Version's practice here is the one that serves a reader best: render what the text has, even when it is awkward, and let the difficulty stand where the Hebrew puts it. A version that quietly tidies its hard places has made itself the authority.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture is not improved by being made smooth. Hard readings are part of what was handed down, and a translation's business is faithfulness, not elegance. Ben-zoheth is a name with a seam in it, and the seam is in the word of God.

pos: n. (a son of Zerubbabel; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Chasadyah, the LORD is kind, from chesed, covenant mercy or lovingkindness, and Yah, the LORD; named once, 1 Chronicles 3:20.
biblical_def: Hasadiah is one of the sons of Zerubbabel: “And Hashubah, and Ohel, and Berechiah, and Hasadiah, Jushabhesed, five” (1 Chronicles 3:20). His father is named in the verse before, with the first group of his children: “And the sons of Pedaiah were, Zerubbabel, and Shimei: and the sons of Zerubbabel; Meshullam, and Hananiah, and Shelomith their sister” (1 Chronicles 3:19). The chapter has brought the royal line through the catastrophe: “And the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son” (1 Chronicles 3:17). What makes this household remarkable is the names in it. Hasadiah means the LORD is kind, and his brother Jushab-hesed means mercy is returned — two sons of the governor of a ruined province, named for covenant mercy, in a generation that had every earthly reason to think God had forgotten. Their father had been given a word of his own: “In that day, saith the LORD of hosts, will I take thee, O Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel, saith the LORD, and will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee, saith the LORD of hosts” (Haggai 2:23).

corruption_summary: Chesed is flattened into a general kindness, where it is the covenant loyalty of God, sworn and binding, and the ground of all assurance.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern renderings and modern preaching often reduce chesed to a warm benevolence — God is nice. The word means something firmer and better: the steadfast covenant love of God, pledged by oath, which He keeps because He has bound Himself to keep it. The Authorized Version's lovingkindness and mercy carry that weight. The difference matters pastorally: a kindly disposition may change with circumstances, and a sworn covenant mercy cannot, which is why the Psalms appeal to it when everything visible has gone wrong.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the courage of these names. Zerubbabel came back to a city in rubble with no crown and a Persian commission, and he called his sons the LORD is kind and mercy is returned. That is faith naming its children after a promise it cannot yet see.

pos: n. (a son of Jeconiah, of the royal line; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Hosham'a, commonly explained as the LORD has heard, a shortened form compounded with Yah and shama', to hear; named once, 1 Chronicles 3:18.
biblical_def: Hoshama occurs once, among the sons of the last king of Judah to be carried away: “Malchiram also, and Pedaiah, and Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah” (1 Chronicles 3:18). The verse before names the father and his heir: “And the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son” (1 Chronicles 3:17). Jeconiah — Jehoiachin — was eighteen when he came to the throne, reigned three months, and spent thirty-seven years in a Babylonian prison before being brought to the king's table. Over him stood one of the heaviest sentences in the prophets: “Thus saith the LORD, Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah” (Jeremiah 22:30). And yet he had sons, six of them named here, and the line went on; the curse was not childlessness in the literal sense but the end of reigning. Matthew takes the line up at that exact point: “And after they were brought to Babylon, Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel” (Matthew 1:12). Hoshama's name means the LORD has heard, and he was born in exile to a king under judgment.

corruption_summary: Prophecy is called falsified when a judgment is not fulfilled in the crudest possible sense, where Jeremiah 22:30 defines its own terms in the verse itself.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah said to write Jeconiah childless, and 1 Chronicles 3:18 names six of his sons; the pair is a favourite exhibit for the claim that biblical prophecy fails. The verse answers the charge in its own second half, which states what the sentence means: that no man of his seed should prosper, sitting on David's throne and ruling in Judah. Childless, in that construction, is dynastic — he would die without an heir who reigned. And so it was: Jeconiah had sons, grandsons and a line running for centuries, and not one of them sat on the throne.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's judgments are exact and His promises survive them. A king under sentence in a Babylonian prison named a son the LORD has heard; the throne stayed empty for five hundred years; and the line was kept until the One came who had a right to it by law and no share in the curse by birth.

pos: n. (head of a Nethinim family that returned from Babylon; also spelt Hasupha, named twice)
etymology: Hebrew Chashupha, commonly explained as stripped or made bare; spelt Hashupha at Nehemiah 7:46 and Hasupha at Ezra 2:43.
biblical_def: This household stands second in the roll of the Nethinims, and the Authorized Version prints the name two ways because the two books do. Nehemiah's register reads: “The Nethinims: the children of Ziha, the children of Hashupha, the children of Tabbaoth” (Nehemiah 7:46); Ezra's reads: “The Nethinims: the children of Ziha, the children of Hasupha, the children of Tabbaoth” (Ezra 2:43). One family, two spellings, the same neighbours on either side — which is how a reader can be sure it is one family, and why the dictionary gives it one entry and names both forms. The Nethinims were the given ones, servants attached to the Levites for the work of the sanctuary, and their appointment is traced back to the monarchy: “Also of the Nethinims, whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites, two hundred and twenty Nethinims: all of them were expressed by name” (Ezra 8:20). They came home and took their places with the rest: “So the priests, and the Levites, and some of the people, and the singers, and the porters, and the Nethinims, dwelt in their cities, and all Israel in their cities” (Ezra 2:70).

corruption_summary: The two registers of the return are called contradictory because their numbers and spellings differ, where each is an accurate copy of a list taken at a different time.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 give the same roll with differences in several totals and spellings, and the pair is pressed hard as proof that the records cannot both be true. The simplest reading accounts for it: Nehemiah says plainly that he found a register of those who came up at the first and copied it, and the two lists were taken at different points — some families arrived later, some numbers were counted differently, and names admitted more than one spelling. Two faithful copies of a living document will differ in exactly these ways and in no doctrinally significant one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God thought the servants' households worth recording twice. A family whose name means stripped came back from Babylon to carry wood and water in the house of the LORD, and both Ezra and Nehemiah wrote them down, second in the list, between Ziha and Tabbaoth.
